newsitem.title: UK: Drought worries dominate European grains markets.
newsitem.headline: Drought worries dominate European grains markets.

text.p: The dry weather has been the main obsession of European grain traders over the past week and looks set to hold centre stage, with no significant rain forecast.
Fears for the developing new crop, hit by drought in some of the most important growing areas, have driven prices higher.

Dealers in Spain said the drought played havoc with prices. LIFFE British wheat futures have risen, led by the new crop. And French traders' fears for the new crop were made worse by a forecast Thursday showing no rain for at least the next week and the imposition of some controls on water abstraction for irrigation.

A lacklustre EU tender did nothing to change the focus of the market. The EU granted licences to 172,300 tonnes of free market wheat at a refund of 6.49 ECUs/tonne and 296,000 tonnes of barley at 29.97 ECUs/tonne.

Even so, the EU reckons it has covered Europe's share of the recent 500,000 tonne Saudi barley purchase. Most, maybe 350,000 to 400,000 tonnes is likely to come from Europe, with the rest from Canada.
French prices for old and new crop firmed, with the weather worries bolstering new crop prices, while continued export optimism helped the old crop.

Algeria bought 100,000 tonnes of optional origin wheat for May/June shipment on Thursday, which French traders expected to come at least partly from France, despite the country's exclusion from recent Algerian purchases.
French operators also cited the rise in British prices and a firm Chicago as bullish factors.
But drought dominated thinking. "A drought psychosis has set in," one French trader said, noting that morning frosts and a dry wind in some areas were just as likely to damage the crop.

The UK market has largely ignored a currency which is at four and a half year highs, as well as potentially bearish new figures on 1996-97 export availability, and leapt ahead on the strength of the weather.
New crop dominated active futures all week and pulled the old crop along with it.

Although the new crop is looking good in most areas, there are reports that some farmers have taken the unusual step of irrigating winter wheat, while others are busy building reservoirs for irrigation.

The UK ministry of agriculture's estimate for UK wheat export availability has been raised to 4.36 million tonnes in the 1996/97 marketing year (July/June) from a previous 4.2 million, the UK's Home Grown Cereals Authority said.

Germany is curiously unscathed by the fashion for drought angst, traders said. It is dry, but the grains market is not getting over-concerned, one explained. Prices in northern Germany are steady, with British rises and rises in Denmark, partly inspired by British buying, putting German supplies in a better position.

There is not a vast amount coming to the market, but it is keeping itself going. "Consumers are getting enough from what is coming forward in the normal course of trade, without having to go back to suppliers and ask them to start looking round for more," one said.
Fob trade was relatively active, he said. And demand for barley was fairly healthy, with trades being done for shipment to Rotterdam and Antwerp, although the amounts available are not great.
Spanish dealers said the continued lack of rain continued to play havoc with ex-farm grain prices.
Wheat was the most affected, and dealers said farmers were holding back supply for fear of crop damage and a reduced harvest.
Feed wheat prices gained 750 pesetas per tonne, while milling wheat jumped 1,000 pesetas.
Trade in durum wheat was non-existent, traders said.
Maize did not react to the lack of rain as it is only just being sown and is grown in irrigated land, dealers said.
Italian durum wheat prices continued their upward trend due to the scarce amount of crop still available on the market and an increase in foreign wheat prices.
